source_text: Inter te et Manichaeum itaque nulla de qualitate naturae, sed de solo est auctore dissensio; hoc enim malum tu Deo reputas, quem parvulorum creatorem fateris, quod Manichaeus principi tenebrarum, quem naturae humanae conditorem putavit. Ad instaurandum igitur foedus non grande vobis remansit obstaculum. Mox tamen docebo, apud utrumque vestrum etsi veritatis vestigia nulla videantur, illius tamen magis quam tua sibimet dicta concinere. Nos porro quid dicimus? Sine dubio, quod utrique vestrum repugnet, id est nec a bono Deo malam nec a principe tenebrarum aliam vel factam vel commixtam esse naturam, sed unum Deum, auctorem rerum omnium, bonam hominum non solum fecisse primum, sed etiam facere in unoquoque nascente naturam, cui tamen creatoris sui opitulationem ut multis modis utilem, ita etiam necessariam profitemur. Quamquam alia est conditionum ratio, alia donorum; nec hic maior operis quam opificis aestimatio vertitur. Ambo igitur, tu et Manichaeus, pariter malum naturale firmatis, id est ambo malam naturam hominum aeque dicitis, sed ille fidelius, tu fraudulentius. Huic enim malo, quod inspiratum a diabolo visceribus humanis pariter arbitramini, nullius ortum ille subducit, tu autem, ut videaris aliquo distare, quod nullum est, solos ab eo duos homines conaris eximere, quorum non tamen personas a peccato liberas, sed provectu eruditioris ingenii dicis in illis non fuisse naturale, quod per illos tamen naturale factum esse persuades. Ita, ne vel istic fraus impunita remaneret, furtum, quod magistro tuo feceras, stultitiae castigavit adiectio; nam credere naturale, quod fatearis de voluntate susceptum, non dico ineruditae, sed ebriae mentis inventum est. Verum hinc alias, nunc interim rem premamus. Affirmat ergo Manichaeus malum esse naturale, tu annuis; dicit peccata nasci, tu ita esse consentis; dicit malam naturam hominum, hoc quoque confirmas; dicit omnium prorsus, hic resistis atque illam primam duorum hominum copulam sequestrari petis, sane quod nec ipsos vindices a reatu, quin immo affirmes mali naturalis auctores. Id si et nos tibi indulgere possimus, tamen tuus non dabit magister, quin forte etiam ferulis in tardum animadvertet ingenium, ita ut tibi necesse sit aut auctoritati acquiescere aut scolas eius omni ex parte deserere. Colligit autem ad extremum et dicit naturae malae bonum auctorem esse non posse ac per hoc principis tenebrarum id est diaboli opus esse hominem, quem naturaliter malum ambo fatemini.
pass_a_gloss: Between you and the Manichaean therefore there is no dissension about the quality of nature, but about the author alone; for this evil you reputate to God, whom you confess the creator of little ones, which the Manichaean to the prince of darkness, whom he thought the founder of human nature. For restoring a treaty therefore not a great obstacle has remained to you. Soon nevertheless I will teach that with both of you, although no traces of truth appear, yet his sayings more than yours agree with themselves. We further what do we say? Without doubt that which fights against both of you, that is neither by the good God an evil nature nor by the prince of darkness another either made or mixed, but one God, author of all things, has not only first made the nature of humans good, but also makes it in each one being born, to which nevertheless we profess the help of its creator as useful in many modes, so also necessary. Although one is the account of conditions, another of gifts; nor here is a greater estimation of the work than of the workman turned. Both therefore, you and the Manichaean, equally establish natural evil, that is both equally say an evil nature of humans, but he more faithfully, you more fraudulently. For from this evil, which you equally judge inspired by the devil into human viscera, he subtracts the rising of no one, but you, that you may seem to differ by something which is nothing, try to exempt only two humans, whose persons nevertheless you do not vindicate from sin, but by the advance of a more learned talent you say in them there was not natural what through them nevertheless you persuade has been made natural. Thus, lest even there fraud remain unpunished, the addition of stupidity has chastised the theft which you had made from your teacher; for to believe natural what you confess taken up from will is an invention not I say of an unlearned but of a drunken mind. But from here elsewhere; now meanwhile let us press the matter. The Manichaean therefore affirms that evil is natural, you nod; he says sins are born, you consent it is so; he says an evil nature of humans, this also you confirm; he says of absolutely all, here you resist and ask that first couple of two humans to be sequestered, indeed which you do not even vindicate from guilt, nay rather you affirm authors of natural evil. If we also could indulge this to you, nevertheless your teacher will not grant it, unless perhaps he will even attend with rods upon a slow talent, so that it is necessary for you either to acquiesce in authority or to desert his schools from every part. He collects however to the extreme and says that a good author of an evil nature cannot be, and through this that a human, whom you both confess naturally evil, is the work of the prince of darkness, that is of the devil.

pass_b_english: Thus between you and Mani there is no disagreement about nature’s character, only about its author. You charge to God, whom you acknowledge as infants’ creator, the same evil Mani charges to the prince of darkness, whom he considered human nature’s maker. Little obstacle remains to renewing your alliance. Soon, however, I shall show that although neither of you shows any trace of truth, his statements agree with one another better than yours do.

What do we say? Undoubtedly something opposed to both of you: neither did the good God make an evil nature, nor did the prince of darkness make or mix another nature. Rather, the one God, author of all things, not only made human nature good at first but also makes it good in every newborn child. Yet we profess the help of its Creator to be both useful in many ways and necessary to it. The making of creatures is one matter and gifts another; and the work is not valued more highly here than the craftsman.

Both you and Mani therefore equally establish natural evil: you both call human nature evil, but he does so more consistently, you more deceitfully. Both of you suppose this evil was breathed by the devil into human inward parts. He exempts no one’s birth from it. You, however, to seem different in some way—although there is no difference—try to exempt just two human beings. Yet you do not free even their persons from sin. With the advance of a more learned intelligence, you say that what you persuade us became natural through them was not natural in them. So, lest your fraud escape punishment even here, the added stupidity punished the theft you committed against your teacher. To believe natural what you admit was adopted by the will is an invention not merely of an uneducated mind but of a drunken one. More about this elsewhere; for now, let us press the matter.

Mani maintains that evil is natural; you agree. He says sins are born; you consent. He says human nature is evil; you confirm this too. He says the nature of absolutely everyone; here you resist, asking that the first pair be set aside. Yet you do not vindicate even them from guilt; rather, you affirm that they originated natural evil. Even if we could indulge you in this, your teacher will not. Perhaps he will even punish your slow intelligence with a schoolmaster’s rod, forcing you either to submit to his authority or to leave his school altogether. Finally he draws his conclusion: an evil nature cannot have a good author. Therefore humanity, which both of you acknowledge to be naturally evil, is the work of the prince of darkness, that is, the devil.
